title: What Would You Say You Do Here?
subtitle: Make your role and scope explicit
summary: A staff engineer is a senior individual contributor whose leverage comes from technical direction, judgment, and helping several teams succeed. The opening chapter asks the reader to describe the work they actually do, align expectations with managers, and treat communication and organizational context as part of the technical role.

concepts.title: Scope
concepts.body: Scope is the boundary of responsibility and influence negotiated with the organization. Agree with your manager on the area you serve, the decisions you are expected to influence, and the gaps you should fill. A title alone does not establish these boundaries, and another company's staff role may be shaped very differently.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A manager and staff engineer write a one-sentence focus before a planning meeting.

concepts.title: Judgment
concepts.body: Technical judgment means choosing under uncertainty while making constraints and consequences explicit. The role combines seeing a bigger picture, executing important work, and raising the capability of others. Choosing which of these needs your attention is part of the work; doing the hardest coding task yourself is not always the most useful contribution.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: During an incident review, the engineer explains why a rollback is safer than a rewrite.

concepts.title: Communication
concepts.body: Communication is part of execution: questions, writing, and explanations move context between people. Your influence extends beyond code you personally change. A clear explanation can help several teams act consistently, while an ambiguous suggestion from a senior person may be mistaken for a decision. Make your intent and the needed action explicit.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A colleague receives a concise design note and can proceed without another meeting.

concepts.title: Role shape
concepts.body: A staff role is an organizational need, not a universal checklist; its shape depends on local gaps. Investigate your reporting chain, scope, preferred work, and current primary focus. These can point in different directions. Naming the mismatch lets you negotiate a useful role instead of trying to imitate a famous staff engineer's career.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A quarterly role check compares stated focus with the requests actually arriving.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Name the role
scenario.context: A platform team asks you to own architecture, unblock releases, and mentor three teams, but your manager measures only your own code output.

options.label: Clarify scope first
options.benefit: Clarifies the decision and creates a workable path through the stated constraint.
options.cost: Negotiation consumes scarce attention and may expose an uncomfortable expectation gap.
options.consequence: You negotiate a written primary focus and success signals; teams know when to involve you.

options.label: Accept every request
options.benefit: Feels faster or safer in the immediate moment and preserves a familiar habit.
options.cost: A broad request queue remains tempting until the next planning cycle.
options.consequence: You appear responsive, but conflicting expectations consume credibility and leave no owner for the hardest work.

scenario.debrief: Both options respond to a real constraint. The stronger choice makes ownership and consequences visible, then creates a point to learn and adjust.

quiz.question: A newly promoted staff engineer receives incompatible requests. What should they clarify first?
options: Which request has the most difficult code
Their expected scope and current primary focus
Which colleague has the oldest ticket
quiz.explanation: The title does not determine the role; scope and organizational needs must be made explicit.

quiz.question: Which contribution fits the broader staff role?
options: Helping several teams make better decisions
Avoiding execution to focus only on strategy
quiz.explanation: The role joins bigger-picture work, execution, and enabling others.

quiz.question: Why might staff engineers at two companies have different jobs?
options: One must be using the title incorrectly
Organizations have different needs and structures
quiz.explanation: Role shape depends on the surrounding organization, not a universal checklist.

exercise.title: Make the next move legible
exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.

fields.label: What is my primary focus?
fields.placeholder: Write the concrete facts, people, and constraint.

fields.label: Which expectation must be renegotiated?
fields.placeholder: State the choice and its trade-off.

fields.label: How will my manager and teams know it is working?
fields.placeholder: Name the evidence or conversation that will revisit it.
